points: Hashing creates a one-way digest; salting adds random uniqueness before hashing to make precomputed attacks harder.

slides.title: Hashing
slides.teach: A one-way transformation that produces a fixed-size digest for a given algorithm.

course.learn: A one-way transformation that produces a fixed-size digest for a given algorithm.

breakdown.explanation: You compare the digest; you do not normally reverse it to recover the original input.

course.why: Hashing supports integrity verification and secure password-storage designs.
course.example: A downloaded file's hash is compared with the publisher's hash.
course.check_q: Which one-way operation is used for integrity checking?

slides.title: Salting
slides.teach: Adds a random value to input before hashing so identical inputs do not produce identical stored hashes.

course.learn: Adds a random value to input before hashing so identical inputs do not produce identical stored hashes.
course.why: It makes precomputed comparisons and rainbow-table attacks less effective.
course.example: Two users with the same password have different stored hashes because each password has a unique salt.
course.check_q: What is added before hashing to make identical passwords produce different hashes?

blocks.title: Encryption, hashing, or salting?
items: Encrypted data is intended to be decrypted by an authorized party.
Example: A file is encrypted and later decrypted with the correct key.
A hash is used for comparison or verification, not normal recovery of the original input.
Example: A file hash is compared with a known-good hash.
A unique salt makes identical passwords produce different hashes.
Example: Two users with the same password still have different stored hash values.
blocks.example: Memory: Encryption = reversible · Hashing = one-way · Salt = random uniqueness.

questions.q: A company compares a downloaded file's digest with the publisher's digest to detect modification. Which cryptographic concept is being used?
questions.explanation: Hashing is commonly used to verify integrity by comparing digests.

questions.q: Two users choose the same password, but their stored password hashes are different because each password has a unique random value added first. What is that value?
questions.explanation: A salt is a random value added before hashing.

questions.q: Which statement best distinguishes hashing from encryption?
choices: Hashing is one-way, while encryption is intended to be reversible with a key
Hashing always uses a public key
questions.explanation: Hashing is one-way; encryption is designed to be decrypted with the proper key.

questions.q: What security benefit does salting provide for stored passwords?
choices: It makes identical passwords produce different hashes
It allows the original password to be decrypted
It replaces the password with a reusable token
It signs the password with a private key
questions.explanation: Unique salts prevent identical passwords from producing identical stored hashes.

questions.q: Which concept is most directly associated with producing a digest used to detect whether data changed?
questions.explanation: Hashing produces digests used in integrity checks.
